title: How we see: light comes into our eyes

summary.text: This unit is about how we see. We can only see when light comes into our eyes. A lamp, the Sun or a fire makes its own light. Most other things, like a mango, a chair or your friend's face, make no light at all. We see them because light bounces off them and travels into our eyes. Inside the eye, a thin layer at the back catches the light and sends signals to the brain. The brain turns those signals into the picture you see. For a long time, people thought eyes sent out rays to touch things. A scientist in Cairo, about a thousand years ago, showed that it works the other way round.
summary.art: A sunlit kitchen: a dotted line of light runs from the window to a mango on the table, bounces off it, and goes into a child's eye, with a small glowing brain behind the eye.

intro.hook: Close your eyes. Now open them. Did something go out of your eyes to fetch the room? Or did something come in?
intro.text: Try one more thing tonight. Go into a room with no light at all, and open your eyes as wide as you can. Wait. Your eyes are working perfectly, and they are wide open. So why can't you see your own hand? This unit is about what your eyes need, and what really happens when you look at something.
intro.art: A child standing in a pitch-dark room with wide-open eyes, their hand held up in front of their face but invisible, only a faint outline drawn.

outcomes: I can say that we see things only when light comes into our eyes.
I can sort things into light sources, which make their own light, and lit things, which only bounce light.
I can draw the path of light from a source, to a thing, and into an eye, with arrows that point the right way.
I can name the main parts of the eye and say what each one does, including the pupil getting bigger and smaller.
I can run a test, show what I found in a table or a bar chart, and say what I think, what I saw, and why.
I can explain why the old idea that eyes send out rays is wrong, using evidence I have seen myself.
I can explain that the brain helps build what we see, and that eyes catch tiny packets of light called photons.
I can say what scientists agree on about seeing, and what nobody knows yet.

terms.meaning: Light is what lets us see. It comes from the Sun, lamps and fires, and travels out from them in every direction.
terms.example: When you switch on a tubelight, its light fills the whole room in a blink.
terms.art: A tubelight on a wall with light spreading out to every corner of a room.

terms.meaning: A thing that makes its own light.
terms.example: The Sun, a diya flame, a torch and a phone screen are light sources.
terms.art: Four small pictures: the Sun, a lit diya, a torch and a glowing phone screen.

terms.meaning: A thing that makes no light of its own. We see it only when light from a source lands on it and bounces off. Scientists call these things non-luminous.
terms.example: A book, a banana, the Moon and your own hand are lit things.
terms.art: A banana on a table in a beam of torchlight, with small arrows bouncing off it.

terms.meaning: Dark means there is no light, or very little. Darkness is not a thing that fills a room. It is what is left when light is missing.
terms.example: When the power goes off at night and there is no moon, the room is dark.
terms.art: A bedroom at night with the lights off, only black, and a child's outline.

terms.meaning: When light hits a thing and comes off it again, we say it bounces. Most things bounce light off in every direction at once.
terms.example: Sunlight bounces off a white wall and makes the whole room brighter.
terms.art: Sunlight from a window hitting a white wall, and many small arrows spraying out from it.

terms.meaning: The part of your body that catches light. It is a ball about as big as a large grape, sitting in a safe hollow in your skull.
terms.example: Your two eyes sit side by side, so each sees the world from a slightly different place.
terms.art: A drawing of a child's face with one eye shown cut open like a ball.

terms.meaning: The black circle in the middle of your eye. It is not a black spot. It is a hole that lets light into the eye.
terms.example: Look in a mirror. The pupil is the round black dot in the middle.
terms.art: A big close-up of an eye with an arrow pointing at the black pupil.

terms.meaning: The coloured ring around the pupil. It is a muscle that makes the pupil hole bigger or smaller.
terms.example: Brown, black, hazel, green and blue eyes are different coloured irises.
terms.art: Five eyes in a row with different coloured irises.

terms.meaning: A clear part just behind the pupil. It helps make the picture sharp at the back of the eye. Another unit explains how lenses work.
terms.example: When an old person has a cataract, their lens has become cloudy, so everything looks misty.
terms.art: A cut-open eye with the clear lens behind the pupil highlighted.

terms.meaning: A thin layer at the back of the inside of the eye. It catches the light that comes in and turns it into signals.
terms.example: The retina is thinner than a page of a notebook, but it holds millions of light-catching cells.
terms.art: A cut-open eye with the back lining shown in pink, covered with tiny dots.

terms.meaning: A thick bundle of nerve threads, like a cable. It carries signals from the eye to the brain.
terms.example: Each eye has its own optic nerve. They meet behind the eyes on the way to the back of the brain.
terms.art: Two eyes with cables running back from them into a brain.

terms.meaning: One small place at the back of each eye that cannot catch light, because the optic nerve leaves the eye there. Everyone has two.
terms.example: You can find your blind spot with a card, a dot and a cross. The dot vanishes!
terms.art: A card with a cross and a dot, and a child covering one eye.

terms.meaning: The two kinds of light-catching cells in the retina. Rods work in dim light. Cones need brighter light and let us see colours.
terms.example: On a dark night, the rods do almost all the work. That is why things look grey at night.
terms.art: A zoomed-in drawing of thin rod cells and pointy cone cells standing side by side.

terms.meaning: The smallest possible bit of light. Light comes in tiny packets, far too small to see one by one. Each packet is a photon.
terms.example: A torch sends out more photons every second than there are grains of sand on all the beaches you have visited.
terms.art: A torch beam drawn as a stream of tiny glowing dots.

terms.meaning: The part of you inside your head that thinks, feels and makes sense of the signals from your eyes.
terms.example: Your eyes catch light, but it is your brain that tells you 'that is Amma's face'.
terms.art: A child's head, see-through, with signals running from the eyes to the back of the brain, where a small picture of a face appears.

terms.meaning: The glow you see in a cat's or a dog's eyes at night when a light shines on them. It is light bouncing back off a shiny layer behind the retina. The eyes are not making light.
terms.example: In a car's headlights, a street dog's eyes can flash green or gold.
terms.art: A street dog at night with two glowing green eyes, caught in a car's headlights.

terms.meaning: A person who finds out how the world works by looking carefully, testing ideas and checking them again.
terms.example: Ibn al-Haytham was a scientist. He tested ideas about seeing with lamps and a dark room.
terms.art: A man in a turban in a dim room, writing next to a small hole of light in a shutter.

explanations.context: This card explains the first big idea of the unit: no light, no seeing.
explanations.definition: We can see a thing only when light from it comes into our eyes. With no light at all, we see nothing, even with our eyes wide open.
explanations.description: Your eyes do not see by themselves. They are light catchers. When there is no light, there is nothing for them to catch. That is why you cannot see your hand in a room with no light at all. As soon as a little light comes in, shapes appear. White and shiny things show first, because they bounce back the most light. Colours come last, because the cells that see colour need more light.
examples: In a power cut on a moonless night, you bump into the furniture you see every day.
In a closed shoebox, a red ball and a white paper are both invisible. Open the lid a crack, and the white paper appears first.
A cave far underground is completely dark. People who explore caves always carry lamps.
explanations.art: Three panels of the same room: totally black, then dim with grey shapes, then bright with full colours.

explanations.context: This card explains the difference between things that make light and things that only bounce it.
explanations.definition: A light source makes its own light. A lit thing makes no light. We see a lit thing only when light from a source lands on it and bounces off into our eyes.
explanations.description: Look around the room. Almost everything you can see is a lit thing. The table, the curtains, your little brother and the cat make no light at all. The only light sources may be a bulb, a window with the Sun outside, or a screen. Everything else is borrowing their light. The Moon looks bright at night, but it is a lit thing too. It is a grey rock with sunlight bouncing off it.
examples: A diya flame is a light source. The brass plate under it is a lit thing that shines with the flame's light.
A phone screen is a light source. Turn it off, and you see the black glass only because the room's light bounces off it.
The Sun is a light source. The Moon is a lit thing.
explanations.art: A table with a lit diya (marked 'makes light') and a brass plate, a book and a cup beside it (marked 'bounces light').

explanations.concept: Light bounces off things and into our eyes
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the whole unit: how we see things that make no light.
explanations.definition: We see a lit thing when light travels from a source to the thing, bounces off it, and then travels into our eyes.
explanations.description: Seeing a lit thing always needs three things. First, a light source. Second, the thing. Third, an eye. The light goes from the source to the thing, then from the thing to the eye. If you break any part of the path, you cannot see the thing. Switch off the lamp, and the path has no start. Hold a card in front of your eyes, and the path has no end. The thing is still there and still lit, but no light from it reaches you.
examples: Sunlight lands on a mango. Some of it bounces off the mango into your eyes, and you see the mango.
A torch shines on a toy. Hold a book between the toy and your eyes. The toy is still lit, but you cannot see it.
At night, a car's headlights land on a cow on the road. The light bounces off the cow into the driver's eyes, just in time.
explanations.art: Three arrows in a chain: the Sun to a mango, the mango to a child's eye, with a small 'X' showing what happens if a hand blocks the second arrow.

explanations.concept: Light bounces off in every direction
explanations.context: This card explains why everyone in a room can see the same chair at the same time.
explanations.definition: Most things bounce light off in every direction at once. So light from them reaches every eye in the room.
explanations.description: Think of a class of children all looking at one blackboard. Each child sees the board. That means light from the board reaches every single child's eyes, in every seat. This happens because rough or matt things, like paper, cloth and skin, spray light out in all directions. A mirror is different. It sends light off in one neat direction, and the reflection unit tells that story. Light you cannot see from the side is another clue. A torch beam in clean air is almost invisible from the side. Clap a dusty duster in it, and the beam appears. Each speck of dust bounces a little of the light sideways, into your eyes.
examples: Everyone at a wedding can see the bride at once, from every side of the hall.
Sunbeams coming through a window show up only where there is dust or smoke in the air.
In a cinema, the light from the projector bounces off the white screen to every seat.
explanations.art: A school classroom seen from above, with dotted lines spraying from the blackboard to every child's eyes.

explanations.concept: Do our eyes send out rays? The 2,000-year argument
explanations.context: This card is about an old idea of seeing, and how people found out it was the wrong way round.
explanations.definition: Light travels from things into our eyes. Our eyes do not send anything out to see.
explanations.description: For more than a thousand years, many clever people thought seeing worked the other way. They thought rays went out of the eyes, like invisible fingers, and touched what we look at. It sounds strange, but it matches how looking feels. We say we 'cast a glance' or 'throw a look'. Many children today still draw arrows coming out of the eyes. Here is how the argument went.
examples: If eyes sent out rays, you would see in a dark room. You can't.
Looking at a very bright light hurts, and leaves a dark blob in your sight afterwards. Something came in and acted on your eye.
Close your eyes and open them at night. The faraway stars appear at once. Could a ray from your eye really reach a star that quickly?

perspectives.who: Empedocles, a Greek thinker, about 2,450 years ago, and later Plato
perspectives.explanation: They thought a kind of fire shines out of the eye, like light from a lantern. When it meets light from the day, we see. Plato knew we need daylight, but he still thought something left the eye.

perspectives.who: Euclid, a Greek mathematician in Alexandria, about 2,300 years ago, and Ptolemy, about 1,900 years ago
perspectives.explanation: They thought straight 'visual rays' go out from the eye in a cone. Whatever the rays touch, we see. They did very good geometry with these rays, even though the rays went the wrong way.

perspectives.who: Aristotle, a Greek thinker, about 2,350 years ago
perspectives.explanation: He disagreed with the eye-rays idea. He thought something travels from the thing we see, through the air, to the eye. He did not have the details right, but the direction was right.

perspectives.who: Ibn al-Haytham, a scientist in Cairo, about 1,000 years ago
perspectives.explanation: He put the pieces together and tested them. Light from a lamp or the Sun lands on things. From every point of a thing, light spreads out in straight lines, and some of it enters the eye. He wrote this in his great Book of Optics, the Kitab al-Manazir. He also said: do not just trust famous books, test them.
Ibn al-Haytham was right about the direction. Light comes into the eye, lands on the retina at the back, and the retina sends signals to the brain. Nothing that helps us see comes out of the eye.

explanations.art: Two pictures side by side: a Greek thinker with dotted rays coming out of his eyes, crossed out, and Ibn al-Haytham with arrows going into his eye from a lamp-lit vase.

explanations.context: This card explains what each part of the eye does, from the front to the back.
explanations.definition: The eye is a ball that lets light in through the pupil, makes a sharp picture with the lens, and catches the light on the retina. The optic nerve carries signals to the brain.
explanations.description: Follow the light into your eye. First it passes through the cornea, a clear window on the front of the eye. Then it goes through the pupil, the black hole in the middle. The pupil looks black because it is a hole into a dark room. Light goes in and hardly any comes back out. Around the pupil is the coloured iris, which makes the hole bigger or smaller. Behind the pupil, the clear lens helps make the picture sharp. The light then crosses the inside of the eye, which is filled with clear jelly. At the back, it lands on the retina. The retina's cells turn light into tiny electric signals. The optic nerve carries those signals to the brain. Eyelids and eyelashes guard the front, and tears keep it clean and wet.
examples: When a doctor shines a light into your eye, she is looking through your pupil at your retina.
In a photo taken with a flash, eyes sometimes look red. The flash bounced off the retina, which is full of tiny blood vessels.
A cataract is a lens that has gone cloudy, so light cannot pass through clearly. Doctors can replace it with a clear plastic lens.
explanations.art: A labelled cut-open eye: eyelid, cornea, iris, pupil, lens, clear jelly, retina, optic nerve, with an arrow of light going in.

explanations.concept: The pupil gets bigger and smaller by itself
explanations.context: This card explains how your eye lets in more light or less light without you deciding.
explanations.definition: In dim light the iris opens the pupil wide to let in more light. In bright light it shrinks the pupil to protect the eye.
explanations.description: Your pupil is like the door of a dark room. In the evening it opens wide, to let in every bit of light it can. In bright sunshine it shrinks to a tiny dot, so that too much light does not dazzle or hurt the retina. You do not have to think about it. It happens in less than a second when a light comes on. Opening up again in the dark is slower, and it takes a few seconds. Doctors check this when someone has hit their head. A pupil that does not change can be a sign that something is wrong.
examples: Come inside from a sunny playground and the room looks dark for a moment, while your pupils open up.
A cat's pupil is a slit. It can close to a thin line in sunshine and open to a big round circle at night.
A goat's pupil is a sideways rectangle. It helps the goat see all around the hillside.
explanations.art: Two close-ups of the same child's eye: one with a tiny pupil in sunshine, one with a huge pupil in a dim room.

explanations.concept: Seeing in the dark: rods, cones and waiting
explanations.context: This card explains why you can see more and more after some time in a dark place, and why no eye can see with no light at all.
explanations.definition: After about 20 to 30 minutes in the dark, the rod cells in the retina become thousands of times more sensitive. But every eye needs at least a little light.
explanations.description: Walk from a bright room into a dark garden at night. At first you see almost nothing. Wait. After a few minutes, shapes appear. After about twenty minutes, you can see paths, trees and many more stars. This is called getting used to the dark. Your pupils open wide quickly, but the bigger change is slower. The rods in your retina slowly build up a special chemical that catches light. Rods are very good in dim light, but they do not see colours. So at night the world looks grey. Bright light uses up the chemical again in a moment. That is why one flash of a phone torch spoils your night eyes.
examples: Astronomers looking at stars use dim red torches, so they do not spoil their night eyes.
Owls have huge eyes packed with rods, so they can hunt by starlight.
A cat sees in much less light than we do. But in a room with no light at all, a cat cannot see either. It uses its whiskers, ears and nose.
explanations.art: A child on a rooftop at night, with three moments: first seeing only a few stars, then more, then the whole sky full of stars after twenty minutes.

explanations.concept: The brain helps make what we see
explanations.context: This card is about the brain's part in seeing. Scientists agree the brain does a lot of the work, but how it makes the picture is still being worked out.
explanations.description: Your eyes catch light, but they do not send a ready-made picture to your brain. They send millions of tiny signals. Your brain puts these together, fills in gaps and decides what you are looking at. Here is proof. Each eye has a blind spot, a place with no light-catching cells at all. You never notice a hole in your sight, because your brain fills it in. Another proof comes from India. Some children were born with cloudy lenses and grew up nearly blind. After an operation, their eyes work. But at first, many cannot match a shape they have felt with their hands to the same shape they see. Their brains have to learn to see, and many of them learn fast. Exactly how a brain turns signals into the picture you see is one of the biggest unanswered questions in science.
examples: Find your blind spot with a cross and a dot on a card. The dot vanishes, but you do not see a hole. You see plain card.
In India, Project Prakash, led by the scientist Pawan Sinha, has helped many children who were born blind to see after surgery. It studies how their brains learn to see.
When you look at clouds, your brain sometimes sees faces and animals that are not really there.
explanations.art: A see-through head: eyes sending a stream of dots back to the brain, where the dots join up into a picture of a cat.

explanations.concept: Light comes in tiny packets, and your eye can catch a few
explanations.context: This card goes down to the smallest bits of light, called photons, and asks how few of them a person can see.
explanations.description: Light comes in tiny packets called photons. A torch sends out billions and billions of them every second. When a photon lands on a rod cell in your retina, it hits one molecule. A molecule is a tiny group of atoms, far too small to see. The photon makes that molecule change its shape, like a bent straw snapping straight. That tiny change starts the signal that goes to your brain. So every time you see anything, it starts with photons bending molecules. Scientists have asked: how few photons can a person notice? Here are the answers so far.
examples: A single rod cell can respond to a single photon. Scientists measured this in the 1970s.
On a dark night, the faint star you can just see may be sending only a few thousand photons into your eye each second.

perspectives.who: Selig Hecht, Simon Shlaer and Maurice Pirenne, in New York, 1942
perspectives.explanation: They sat people in total darkness and flashed very dim lights at them. A person could notice a flash when only about 5 to 14 photons were caught in the eye. So the eye is close to as sensitive as anything can be.

perspectives.who: Alipasha Vaziri and his team of scientists, 2016
perspectives.explanation: They used a special light source that could send exactly one photon at a time. Their volunteers guessed a little better than chance when a single photon had arrived. So maybe a person can sometimes sense just one photon.

They say the single-photon result was small, and needs to be repeated by other teams before everyone accepts it. Nobody doubts that rod cells can catch one photon. The question is whether the whole person notices.

explanations.art: A single tiny glowing dot travelling into a giant eye and striking one curly molecule at the back, which straightens like a spring.

explanations.concept: Many kinds of eyes, and seeing without eyes
explanations.context: This card goes out from our eyes to the eyes of other living things, and to living things that sense light with no eyes at all.
explanations.definition: Living things have many different kinds of eyes, and some sense light with no eyes at all. All of them work by catching light that comes in.
explanations.description: Our eyes are not the only design. A spider has eight eyes. A scallop, a kind of shellfish, can have up to two hundred tiny eyes along the edge of its shell. Each scallop eye uses a curved mirror at the back, made of tiny crystals, instead of a lens. A box jellyfish has twenty-four eyes. Scientists think eyes have appeared many separate times in the history of life. But every kind of eye works the same basic way. Light comes in, and a molecule catches it. Even living things with no eyes sense light. A money plant on a windowsill bends towards the window. Tiny one-celled living things in a pond swim towards light, using a little light-sensing spot.
examples: A dragonfly's eyes are made of thousands of tiny eyes packed together.
A sunflower bud turns to follow the Sun across the sky. It has no eyes, but it senses light.
Earthworms have no eyes, but their skin can sense light. They wriggle away from it.
explanations.art: A circle of different eyes: a human eye, a spider's eight eyes, a scallop's row of blue dots, a dragonfly's bumpy eye, and a plant bending towards a window.

explanations.concept: Do we see the world as it really is?
explanations.context: This card is a big question that scientists and thinkers still argue about: is what we see the world itself, or a picture our brain makes?
explanations.description: When you look at a tree, it feels as if you are seeing the tree itself, right there. But we know that light bounced off the tree, came into your eyes, became signals, and your brain built the picture. So what are you really seeing? People give different answers.
examples: A bee sees patterns on flowers that our eyes cannot catch. Which flower is the real one, the bee's or ours?
Two people can look at the same picture and see different things, like a duck or a rabbit.

perspectives.who: Many people, most of the time
perspectives.explanation: We see the world as it is. The tree is green and leafy, and that is what we see.

perspectives.who: Anil Seth, a British neuroscientist, in his book Being You, 2021
perspectives.explanation: The brain is always guessing what is out there. It checks its guesses against the signals from the eyes. What we see is the brain's best guess, which is usually very good.

perspectives.who: James Gibson, an American scientist who studied seeing, 1979
perspectives.explanation: We do not need a picture inside the head. The light coming into our eyes already carries rich information about the world, and we pick it up directly as we move around.

explanations.art: A tree outside a window, and a child looking at it, with a thought bubble showing a slightly different tree, and a question mark between them.

agreed.text: We see things only when light from them enters our eyes.
agreed.evidence: In complete darkness nobody sees anything, even with healthy eyes wide open. Block the light between a thing and your eyes, and the thing disappears from view.

agreed.text: Most things make no light. We see them because they bounce light from a source into our eyes.
agreed.evidence: Switch off the lamp in a closed room, and the table, the books and your hand all vanish together. Switch it on, and they all appear together.

agreed.text: The retina at the back of the eye turns light into signals, and the optic nerve carries them to the brain.
agreed.evidence: Doctors can look at the retina through the pupil. Scientists have measured the tiny electric signals that retina cells make when light lands on them.

agreed.text: The pupil gets bigger in dim light and smaller in bright light, by itself.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can watch it happen in a mirror. Doctors check it with a small torch.

agreed.text: Rod cells can respond to a single photon, and after time in the dark our eyes become much more sensitive.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have measured single rod cells catching single photons. Tests in dark rooms show that what people can see improves for about half an hour.

challenging.claim: Our eyes send out rays that touch what we look at.
challenging.who: Empedocles, Plato, Euclid and Ptolemy in ancient Greece and Egypt. Many children today still draw arrows coming out of the eyes.
challenging.for: Looking feels like something we do, reaching out to the world. We turn our eyes to point at things, a bit like pointing a torch.
challenging.against: If eyes sent out rays, we would see in the dark. Bright light hurts the eye, which shows something comes in. About 1,000 years ago, Ibn al-Haytham put these clues together, and today we can measure the light landing on the retina.
challenging.context: This card is about the oldest wrong idea about seeing, and why scientists gave it up.

challenging.claim: If you wait long enough in a totally dark room, you will start to see.
challenging.who: Many people believe this, because their eyes do get better in the dark after a while.
challenging.for: In a dim room, your eyes really do get much more sensitive after twenty minutes. Things that were invisible appear.
challenging.against: That only works when there is a little light, like starlight or a crack under the door. In a room with no light at all, there is nothing for the eye to catch. No amount of waiting helps.
challenging.context: This card is about a common belief about seeing in the dark.

challenging.claim: Cats can see in complete darkness.
challenging.who: A very common belief, because cats' eyes glow at night and cats move easily in dim light.
challenging.for: Cats really can see in about one-sixth of the light we need. Their pupils open very wide, and a shiny layer behind the retina gives light a second chance to be caught.
challenging.against: The glow is light bouncing back, not light made by the eye. With no light at all, a cat sees nothing. It finds its way with its whiskers, ears and nose.
challenging.context: This card is about a belief about cats' eyes.

challenging.claim: Eating lots of carrots lets you see in the dark.
challenging.who: A story spread in Britain during the Second World War, about pilots who ate carrots.
challenging.for: Carrots have something the body turns into vitamin A. The rod cells need vitamin A, and people who badly lack it get night blindness. Eating carrots and green leafy vegetables really does fix that.
challenging.against: If your body already has enough vitamin A, extra carrots will not give you better night vision than normal. The wartime story also helped keep secret that the pilots were really using radar.
challenging.context: This card is about a famous food myth about seeing.

challenging.claim: People can feel when someone is staring at the back of their head.
challenging.who: Many people feel this is true. The biologist Rupert Sheldrake has run tests that he says support it.
challenging.for: Most of us have turned around and found someone looking at us. Sheldrake reported results a little better than chance.
challenging.against: Nothing comes out of the eyes to be felt. We remember the times we turned and someone was looking, and forget the times nobody was. Other scientists who ran careful tests found no effect.
challenging.context: This card is about a belief that looking sends something out, like the old eye-rays idea.

challenging.claim: The eye works just like a camera, and the brain simply looks at the photo.
challenging.who: A common way of explaining eyes in books and classrooms.
challenging.for: The eye and a camera both have a hole that lets light in, something to make the picture sharp, and a layer at the back that catches the light.
challenging.against: There is no little person inside the head looking at a photo. The brain builds what we see from signals, fills in the blind spot, and guesses. People who gain sight as children have to learn to see shapes.
challenging.context: This card is about whether 'the eye is a camera' is a good way to think about seeing.

big_questions.q: When you look at a mango, is the mango coming into you, or are you going out to the mango?
big_questions.hint: Think about what travels. Where did the light start, and where did it end up?

big_questions.q: If nobody is in the room and the light is on, is the chair still being seen?
big_questions.hint: Light is still bouncing off the chair. Is bouncing the same as seeing?

big_questions.q: Why can't you see your own eyes without a mirror or a photo?
big_questions.hint: For you to see something, its light has to travel into your eyes. Where would the light from your eye have to go?

big_questions.q: Is a colour in the mango, in the light, or in your brain?
big_questions.hint: In a dark room, does the mango still have a colour? Ask again after the colour unit.

big_questions.q: Your brain fills in your blind spot. What else might your brain be filling in without telling you?
big_questions.hint: Remember the vanishing dot. You saw plain card where there was really a dot.

big_questions.q: People who are blind know the world through sound, touch and smell. Is their world smaller than yours, or just different?
big_questions.hint: Think of what a blind person might notice that you miss.

big_questions.q: Ibn al-Haytham said do not just believe famous books. Test them. Is there something everyone believes that you would like to test?
big_questions.hint: He tested what Euclid and Ptolemy wrote, even though they were famous.

big_questions.q: If two people look at the same sunset, do they see the same thing?
big_questions.hint: The light is the same, but each person's eyes and brain are their own.

big_questions.q: When you look at someone and they look at you, what is travelling between you?
big_questions.hint: Light bounces off your face into their eyes, and off their face into yours.

story.title: The Lamp-Seller's Daughter
story.note: Ibn al-Haytham was real. He lived in Cairo and wrote the Book of Optics, the Kitab al-Manazir. In it he describes lamps placed outside a small hole into a dark room, and how covering one lamp makes its spot of light on the wall vanish. Later writers tell the story that he pretended to be mad so the Caliph al-Hakim would not punish him, and was kept in his house until the Caliph died in 1021. Historians are not sure that story is true. Zaynab, her father and their conversations are made up.
text: In the city of Cairo, a thousand years ago, there was a house that everybody walked past quickly. The shutters were always closed. People said a madman lived inside. They said he had once been a great scholar. He had promised the Caliph he could tame the river Nile. Then he had failed, and his mind had broken.
Zaynab was ten. Every Friday she carried a jar of lamp oil to that house, because her father sold oil and the madman's servant paid well. She always set the jar down by the door and ran.
Her grandmother had warned her. "Never let a madman look at you," she said. "Eyes throw out rays, like a lamp throws out light. A strange man's eyes can reach out and touch you."
Zaynab believed it. Everyone did. Even the old books said so. The great Greek teachers had written that we see by sending invisible rays out of our eyes, like long thin fingers.
One Friday, the servant was ill, and the door was open. A voice called from inside. "Bring the oil in, please. I will not bite."
Zaynab stood still. Then, because she was curious, which was always her trouble, she stepped inside.

The room was dark. Not dim, but truly dark, like the inside of a closed fist. She could not see her own hand. She could not see the jar she was holding. Somewhere in the blackness, a man was breathing.
"Can you see me?" said the voice.
"No," said Zaynab.
"But your eyes are open?"
"Wide open."

"Then where are your rays?" said the voice. It did not sound mad. It sounded amused. "If your eyes threw out rays to touch things, they would touch me now. The dark would not stop them. Yet you see nothing. Why?"
Zaynab had no answer. She waited for her eyes to work. They did not.
"Here," said the voice. There was a scrape, and a thin bar of the shutter slid aside. A hole no bigger than a coin opened, high on the wall.
And something happened that Zaynab never forgot.

On the white wall opposite the hole, a picture appeared. It was faint and soft, as if painted in smoke. But it was the street outside. There was the fruit seller's yellow awning. There was a donkey, and a man leading it. They were upside down, and they were moving. The donkey walked slowly across the wall on its head.
Zaynab cried out. "Is it magic?"

"It is light," said the man. Now she could see him a little, by the glow from the wall. He was thin, with ink on his fingers and a gentle face. "The sun lands on the donkey. From every part of the donkey, light bounces off and spreads out in all directions. A little of that light comes through my hole and lands on my wall. The light comes from the donkey to us. Nothing goes from us to the donkey."
"But the old books say..."
"The old books say many things." He smiled. "Euclid was a great man. Ptolemy was a great man. I have read every word they wrote. But a book is not a lamp. A lamp you can test."

He took her oil and filled three small lamps. He set them on a shelf outside the second shutter, side by side. Then he closed the room again, leaving only one small hole. On the wall inside, three little spots of light appeared, one for each lamp.
"Now," he said, "go outside and put your hand in front of the first lamp."
She did. When she came back, he told her. One spot had gone out while her hand was there. Only that one. The other two had glowed on.

"Each lamp sends its own light," he said. "It travels through the hole to the wall. Block the lamp, and its light never arrives. My eyes are like this room, little lamp-seller. They are dark rooms with a small hole in front. The light of the world comes in. I do not reach out for it. I wait for it, and I catch it."
Zaynab thought about this all the way home. She thought about her grandmother, and the rays, and the madman's eyes.

That night there was no moon. She lay on the roof and looked at the stars. Before, she had thought her eyes were reaching all the way out to them, like fingers stretching across the sky. Now she knew it was the other way round. Light from each star had come all that way and dropped into her eyes. Tiny lamps, so far away, were sending her their light.
She closed her eyes. The stars vanished. She opened them, and the stars were back. Her eyes had done nothing but open the door.

Every Friday after that, Zaynab went inside. The man showed her how a bright light hurts the eye and leaves a dark blob floating in your sight. "Something came in and pressed on you," he said. "Eyes are touched by light. They do not touch." He showed her how a dusty sunbeam glows only where the dust is.

One day the servant told her the Caliph had died. A few weeks later, the shutters of the house stood wide open. The man was gone. People said he had never been mad at all. He had only pretended, to stay alive. In the quiet years in the dark room, he had been writing a book.

It was called the Book of Optics. Two hundred years later it was carried across the sea and copied into Latin. Scholars in Europe read it for centuries. They learned from it how light comes into the eye.
Zaynab never saw him again. But she sold lamp oil all her life. And whenever a child came to her stall, she would hold up a lamp and ask a question.
"Tell me," she would say. "When you look at this flame, who is doing the reaching? You, or the light?"
story.epiphany: For the parent: the turn of the story is a dark room. With her eyes wide open, Zaynab sees nothing, so eyes cannot be sending out rays. When a small hole lets light in, the street appears on the wall, because light bounced off the donkey and travelled in. Covering one lamp makes only its spot vanish, which shows that each light travels separately from its source to where it lands. Seeing is catching light that comes in, not reaching out. The story also asks whether to trust a famous book or a test, and it quietly turns the 'madman' everyone avoided into the person who knew most.
ask: In the dark room, Zaynab's eyes were wide open. Why couldn't she see anything?
What made the picture of the street appear on the wall?
When Zaynab blocked one lamp, what happened? What does that show about where light goes?
Zaynab's grandmother believed that eyes throw out rays. What would you say to her, kindly?
People called the man mad and walked past his house quickly. Why do you think they were wrong about him?

games.title: Light Chain
games.players: 2 to 4 players, or one child playing against the app
games.context: Light Chain is a card game about how we see. To see a thing, you need a light source, the thing, and an eye, joined in a chain.

printables.title: 12 THING cards to cut out
items: A sari on a washing line

printables.title: 8 EYE cards and 10 BLOCKER cards
items: BLOCKER: a hand over the eyes
BLOCKER: a blanket over your head
BLOCKER: a cloud over the Sun

printables.title: A chain mat with three boxes and two arrows

rules: Cut out all the cards. Shuffle the SOURCE, THING and EYE cards into one pile. Keep the BLOCKER cards in a separate pile.
Each player takes 5 cards from the main pile.
On your turn, take one more card. If you can, lay down a full chain: one SOURCE, one THING and one EYE, in that order, on the chain mat.
Say the chain out loud: 'Light goes from the torch to the cat, and bounces off the cat into Grandpa's eye. So Grandpa sees the cat.' A correct chain wins 2 seeing tokens.
After a chain is laid, the next player can take a BLOCKER card and put it on one arrow. They say how it breaks the chain. A good reason wins 1 token, and the chain is out.
A SOURCE card can also be laid straight to an EYE, with no THING. Then you are seeing the light source itself. This wins 1 token.
When the main pile runs out, the player with the most tokens wins.

flow.do: 1. Lay the chain mat on the floor. 2. Shuffle the SOURCE, THING and EYE cards into one pile. 3. Put the BLOCKER cards in their own pile. 4. Deal 5 cards to each player.
flow.say: To see something, light has to make a journey. It starts at a light source, bounces off the thing, and ends in an eye. In this game you build those journeys with cards.
flow.kid: Put the chain mat on the floor. Mix the cards, but keep the BLOCKER cards apart. Take 5 cards each. You will build light's journey: source, thing, eye.
flow.context: This is the first step of Light Chain. It is a card game where you build the path light takes when we see something. Here you set up the game.

flow.do: Play one practice chain together. Lay down 'A torch', then 'A cat', then 'Grandpa's eye'. Point along the arrows as you say it.
flow.say: Here is a practice chain. The torch makes light. The light lands on the cat and bounces off it. Some of it goes into Grandpa's eye. So Grandpa sees the cat.
flow.kid: Practice chain: a torch, a cat, Grandpa's eye. Light goes from the torch to the cat. It bounces into Grandpa's eye. Which way do the arrows point?

check.q: In the chain 'torch, cat, Grandpa's eye', which way does the light go between the cat and Grandpa?
options: From Grandpa's eye to the cat
From the cat into Grandpa's eye
Both ways at once
check.why: Light bounces off the cat and travels into Grandpa's eye. That is how he sees the cat. Picking 'from Grandpa's eye to the cat' is the very old idea that eyes send out rays. Ibn al-Haytham showed it is the other way round. Picking 'both ways' is close to how looking feels, but nothing that helps us see leaves the eye.

flow.do: 1. Take turns. Each player takes a card and lays a chain if they can. 2. They say the chain out loud. 3. Give 2 tokens for a correct chain.
flow.say: When you lay a chain, say where the light starts, what it bounces off, and whose eye it ends in.
flow.kid: Take a card. Can you make a chain? Say it out loud. Where does the light start? What does it bounce off? Whose eye does it go into?
flow.parent: Watch for chains in the wrong order, like THING first. Ask: 'Does a mango make its own light?' Watch the Moon card too. The Moon is a THING, not a SOURCE, because it only bounces sunlight. The firefly is a SOURCE. It makes its own light. The camera works like an eye: light comes in and is caught.

ask.q: Why is the Moon a THING card and not a SOURCE card?
good: The Moon makes no light of its own.

flow.do: When a chain is laid, let the next player put a BLOCKER card on one of its arrows. They say which part of the journey is broken.
flow.say: Blocker time. Put your blocker on an arrow. Tell us which part of the light's journey it breaks.
flow.kid: Got a BLOCKER card? Put it on one arrow. Which part of the journey does it break? Say why.

check.q: A 'power cut' blocker is played on the chain 'tubelight, book, your eye'. Which part does it break?
options: The start: the tubelight makes no light
The end: your eye stops working
Nothing, you can still see the book
check.why: In a power cut the tubelight goes off. So there is no light to land on the book, and nothing to bounce into your eye. The eye is fine, and so is the book. Picking 'your eye stops working' usually means thinking the eye does the seeing on its own. Picking 'you can still see' means forgetting that lit things need a source.

flow.do: Count the tokens. Then ask the closing question.
flow.say: Count your seeing tokens. Who won? Now think back over all the chains. Which way did every arrow point?
flow.kid: Count your tokens. Who has the most? Now look at all the arrows. Which way did they all point?
flow.think: Can you think of anything you can see that is not at the end of a chain like this?
flow.parent: Every arrow points towards an eye. That is the big idea of the unit. Seeing is light arriving.

setup.art: Three printed cards laid in a row on a chain mat: a torch card, a cat card and an eye card, with two arrows between them.
setup.caption: 1. Lay a chain: SOURCE, then THING, then EYE.

setup.art: A child's hand laying a 'thick curtain' BLOCKER card on the arrow between the cat card and the eye card.
setup.caption: 2. Break a chain with a BLOCKER card, and say why.

setup.art: A pile of small paper eye tokens being counted by two children.
setup.caption: 3. Count your seeing tokens at the end.

games.title: Photon Relay
games.players: 4 or more players, best with a family or friends
games.context: Photon Relay is an act-out game. Players become the Sun, a thing and an eye, and carry balls of 'light' between them to show how we see.

printables.title: Role cards to wear on a string
Relay record
items: How many light balls reached the EYE
Did the BRAIN guess the thing?

rules: One player is the SUN, one is the MANGO, one is the EYE and one is the BRAIN. Others can be CLOUDS.
The SUN holds a basket of balls or rolled-up yellow socks. Each one is a little bit of light, a photon.
The SUN throws light balls gently towards the MANGO. The MANGO catches them and throws them on in any direction. This is bouncing.
The EYE stands with a basket held in front of them. It cannot move its feet. It only catches the balls that come its way.

Each ball that lands in the EYE's basket is passed back to the BRAIN, who stands behind the EYE with closed eyes. The MANGO whispers one clue word with each ball, like 'yellow' or 'round'. The BRAIN guesses what the thing is.
CLOUDS can step between the SUN and the MANGO to block light. Then nothing reaches the EYE.

flow.do: 1. Give out the role cards. 2. Put the SUN at one end of the room, the MANGO in the middle, and the EYE to one side of the MANGO. 3. The BRAIN stands behind the EYE.
flow.say: We are going to act out how you see a mango. Each sock ball is a tiny bit of light. Scientists call one tiny bit of light a photon.
flow.kid: Pick a role: SUN, MANGO, EYE or BRAIN. The socks are bits of light. Get in your places.
flow.context: This is the first step of Photon Relay. Players act out light travelling from the Sun, to a mango, to an eye. Here everyone takes a role.

flow.do: 1. The SUN throws sock balls gently to the MANGO, one at a time. 2. The MANGO throws each one on in any direction, without aiming. 3. The EYE catches what it can and passes it to the BRAIN.
flow.say: SUN, send your light. MANGO, bounce it anywhere, don't aim. EYE, you can only catch what comes to you. You cannot reach out.
flow.kid: SUN, throw the light gently. MANGO, bounce it any way at all. EYE, stand still and catch. Pass what you catch to the BRAIN.
flow.parent: Throw softly, with socks, not hard balls. The point is that the EYE catches only a few of the bounced balls. Most go off in other directions, which is why everyone in a room can see the same mango.

flow.do: Ask the BRAIN to guess what the thing is from the clue words that came with each caught ball.
flow.say: BRAIN, you only know what the EYE caught. What do you think the thing is?
flow.kid: BRAIN, listen to the clues that came with your balls. What is the thing?

ask.q: Why did the EYE not catch every ball?
good: The mango bounced them every way.
The eye only catches what comes towards it.

check.q: In Photon Relay, what does the EYE do?
options: It throws balls out to the mango
It catches the balls that come to it
It makes its own balls
check.why: A real eye catches light that comes into it. It does not send anything out, and it makes no light of its own. Picking 'throws balls out' is the old eye-rays idea. Picking 'makes its own balls' mixes the eye up with a light source, like a torch.

flow.do: Play one more round. This time a CLOUD steps between the SUN and the MANGO halfway through.
flow.say: Now the CLOUD comes. What happens to the light reaching the EYE?
flow.kid: CLOUD, step in front of the SUN. What happens now? Does the EYE still get any light?
flow.think: The MANGO is still there when the cloud comes. Why can't the EYE see it?

flow.do: Sit down together and ask your child to say what they think, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Let's finish like scientists. What do you think now about how we see? What did you see in the game that shows it? And why does it work that way?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: we see when light comes into our eyes. What I saw: the EYE only knew about the mango when balls landed in its basket. Why: the mango makes no light, so it has to bounce light from the Sun to the eye.

setup.art: A living room with four children wearing paper role cards: SUN at one end with a basket of rolled yellow socks, MANGO in the middle, EYE to one side holding a basket.
setup.caption: 1. Take roles: SUN, MANGO, EYE and BRAIN.

setup.art: The SUN child tossing a sock ball to the MANGO child, who tosses it on sideways towards the EYE child's basket.
setup.caption: 2. The SUN sends light. The MANGO bounces it any way.

setup.art: A child as a grey CLOUD stepping between the SUN and the MANGO, with sock balls bouncing off the cloud.
setup.caption: 3. A CLOUD blocks the light, and the EYE gets nothing.

items.p: What do we need to see a book?
opts: Light from the book coming into our eyes
Our eyes sending rays to the book
items.why: We see a book when light bounces off it into our eyes. Picking 'eyes sending rays' is the very old idea that eyes reach out to see. Picking 'only our eyes' forgets that in a dark room even healthy eyes see nothing.
items.art: A child reading a book by a window, with arrows from the window to the book to the eye.

items.p: Which one is a light source?
items.why: A light source makes its own light. A lit candle does. The Moon, a mirror and a steel plate only bounce light from somewhere else. Picking the Moon is very common, because it looks so bright at night. But it is a rock lit by the Sun.

items.p: Things that make their own light are called light ____.
items.why: A light source makes its own light, like the Sun, a bulb or a fire.

items.p: Sort these. Does it make its own light, or does it only bounce light?
items.why: Light sources make their own light. Everything else we see, including the Moon and the white wall, only bounces light that came from a source.

items.p: In a room with no light at all, you can see if you open your eyes very wide.
items.why: False. Wide-open eyes still need light to catch. With no light, there is nothing to see. The dark box test showed this.

items.p: You are in the dark box test. The lid is shut. What do you see through the peephole?
items.why: With the lid sealed, no light gets in, so no light can bounce off the things into your eye. Picking 'the white paper only' is what happens when a crack of light comes in. Picking 'everything in grey' is how things look in dim light, not in no light.

items.p: In the dark box test, which thing do you usually see first when a little light comes in?
opts: They all appear at the same moment
items.why: White things bounce back the most light, so they show up first. Picking the red ball usually means thinking bright colours show best in the dark. In dim light, colours are the last thing we see.

items.p: Put the light's journey in order, so that you see a mango.
items: The light lands on the mango.
items.why: Light starts at a source, lands on the thing, bounces off it, enters the eye, and the eye sends signals to the brain.

items.p: Match each part of the eye to what it does.
pairs: a hole that lets light in
makes the pupil bigger or smaller
catches the light at the back of the eye
items.why: Light goes in through the pupil. The iris changes its size. The retina catches the light. The optic nerve carries the signals to the brain.

items.p: Why does the pupil look black?
opts: It is a hole, and very little light comes back out of it
It is the darkest part of the iris
items.why: The pupil is a hole into the dark inside of the eye. Light goes in and hardly any comes back out, so it looks black. Picking 'painted black' is a common idea, but there is no paint. Picking 'darkest part of the iris' mixes up the coloured ring with the hole in the middle.
items.art: A close-up of an eye with the pupil labelled 'a hole'.

items.p: You come in from a sunny playground into a dim room. What do your pupils do?
opts: Get bigger, to let in more light
Get smaller, to keep light out
items.why: In dim light the pupils open wide to catch as much light as they can. Picking 'get smaller' is what happens when you go into bright light. Picking 'stay the same' misses that the pupil changes by itself.

items.p: The black circle in the middle of your eye is called the ____.
items.why: The pupil is the hole in the middle of the iris. Light enters the eye through it.

items.p: Draw a lamp, a ball and an eye. Draw arrows to show how the eye sees the ball.
items.a: One arrow goes from the lamp to the ball. Another arrow goes from the ball into the eye.
items.why: Light goes from the source to the thing, then bounces into the eye. No arrow comes out of the eye.
items.art: A blank space with small outlines of a lamp, a ball and an eye.

items.p: The Moon makes its own light.
items.why: False. The Moon is a rock. We see it because sunlight bounces off it into our eyes.

items.p: A torch is shining on a toy, but you hold a book in front of your eyes. Why can't you see the toy? Use the word 'light' in your answer.
items.a: The light that bounces off the toy cannot reach my eyes, because the book is in the way. The toy is still lit, but no light from it comes into my eyes.
items.why: Seeing needs the whole journey: source, then thing, then eye. Breaking any part stops you seeing.

items.p: Which of these helps you see in the dark?
opts: Waiting about 20 minutes in a dim place, away from bright lights
items.why: After about 20 minutes in dim light, the rod cells in your eyes get much more sensitive. Picking carrots is a famous myth. Carrots keep eyes healthy, but extra carrots do not give normal eyes night vision. Picking 'staring hard' doesn't help, because the eye can only catch light that comes in.

items.p: Everyone in a classroom can see the blackboard at once. Why?
opts: The board bounces light off in every direction, so light reaches every child
Each child's eyes send a ray to the board
The board makes its own light
items.why: Matt surfaces like a blackboard spray light in all directions. So some light from the board reaches every seat. Picking 'eyes send a ray' is the old eye-rays idea. Picking 'makes its own light' mixes a lit thing up with a light source.

items.p: A torch beam crosses a dark room. It is hard to see from the side, until mist is sprayed into it. Why does the mist help?
opts: Mist drops bounce some of the light sideways into your eyes
Mist slows the light down so you can see it
items.why: We only see light that comes into our eyes. Without mist, the beam goes straight to the wall. Mist drops bounce a little light every way, and some reaches you. Picking 'mist makes light' mixes up a lit thing with a source. Picking 'slows the light down' is a guess, but speed was never the reason.

items.p: A cat's eyes glow in the dark because they make their own light.
items.why: False. The glow is light from a torch or headlight bouncing off a shiny layer at the back of the cat's eye. With no light at all, a cat's eyes do not glow.

items.p: In the blind spot activity, the dot vanished. What did you see in its place?
opts: Plain white card, because the brain filled it in
items.why: The blind spot has no light-catching cells. But the brain fills the gap with what is around it, so you see plain card. Picking 'a black hole' is what many people expect. It shows how hard the brain works without telling us.

items.p: Long ago, many people believed that eyes send out rays to touch what we see. Give two pieces of evidence that this is wrong.
items.a: First, in a totally dark room we see nothing, even with our eyes open. If eyes sent out rays, we would still see. Second, looking at a very bright light hurts and leaves a dark blob in our sight, which shows something came into the eye.
items.why: Ibn al-Haytham used clues like these. Another good answer: when one lamp is covered, only its spot of light vanishes.

items.p: Which part of the eye turns light into signals for the brain?
items.why: The retina at the back of the eye has millions of light-catching cells, the rods and the cones. They turn light into signals. The iris only changes the size of the pupil, and the eyelid protects the eye.

items.p: Match each living thing to how it senses light.
pairs: up to 200 small eyes with tiny mirrors
no eyes, but it bends towards the window
huge eyes full of rod cells
items.why: Living things sense light in many ways, but all of them catch light that comes in.

items.p: The cells in the retina that work best in dim light are called ____.
items.why: Rods work in dim light but do not see colours. Cones need brighter light and see colours.

items.p: Why do astronomers use red torches when looking at stars?
opts: Red light disturbs their night eyes less than white light
items.why: A bright white light quickly undoes the 20 minutes your rod cells spent getting used to the dark. Red light disturbs the rods much less. Picking 'red light is brighter' gets it backwards. The point is to use a dim light.

items.p: The smallest bit of light is called a photon.
items.why: True. Light comes in tiny packets called photons. A rod cell in your eye can respond to just one.

items.p: Put these in order from the front of the eye to the back.
items.why: Light passes through the clear cornea, then the pupil, then the lens, then the jelly that fills the eye, and lands on the retina at the back.

items.p: In Ibn al-Haytham's lamps activity, you covered one torch. What happened?
opts: Only that torch's spot went out
items.why: Each torch sends its own light through the hole. Block one, and only its light stops arriving. This shows light travels from each source to where it lands.

items.p: Your friend says, 'I can see the Moon, so the Moon must make light.' What would you tell your friend?
items.a: We can see many things that make no light, like a book or a face. We see them because light bounces off them into our eyes. The Moon is like that. Sunlight bounces off it to us.
items.why: Seeing a thing does not mean it makes light. Most things we see are lit things.

items.p: In the Eye in a Box project, which pupil made the brightest picture on the retina screen?
items.why: A bigger hole lets in more light, so the screen glows brighter. That is why your pupil opens wide in the dark.

items.p: Draw a cat in the dark with glowing eyes, and a person holding a torch. Draw arrows to show where the glow comes from.
items.a: An arrow from the torch to the cat's eye, and an arrow bouncing back from the cat's eye to the person.
items.why: Eyeshine is torchlight bouncing back from a shiny layer inside the cat's eye. No arrow should start inside the cat's eye.
items.art: Outlines of a cat and a person holding a torch, in a dark lane.

worksheets.title: How we see: thinking like Ibn al-Haytham

items.p: Ibn al-Haytham said do not just trust famous books, test them. Describe a test that would show a friend that eyes do not send out rays.
items.a: Sit my friend in a totally dark room with eyes open, and ask what they see. Nothing. Then let in a little light, and things appear. If eyes sent out rays, they would see in the dark too.
items.why: A good test changes one thing, the light, and keeps the eyes the same.

items.p: Selig Hecht and his team found that people can notice a flash when only a few photons are caught. What does this tell us?
opts: The eye is extremely sensitive to light
The eye needs huge amounts of light
items.why: Catching only about 5 to 14 photons is close to the smallest amount of light there can be. So the eye is one of the most sensitive light detectors we know. Picking 'huge amounts' gets it backwards. Picking 'photons are big' is wrong, because photons are far too small to see one by one.

items.p: Scientists all agree that a person can notice a single photon.
items.why: False. Rod cells can respond to one photon. One 2016 study suggested a person can sometimes notice a single photon, but other scientists want it repeated before they agree.

items.p: Children who were born blind and had an operation to clear their cloudy lenses often could not, at first, match a shape they had felt with their hands to the same shape seen with their eyes. What does this tell us about seeing?
items.a: Seeing is not only done by the eyes. The brain has to learn to make sense of the signals. Their eyes worked after the operation, but their brains still needed time to learn.
items.why: This was studied in India by Project Prakash, led by Pawan Sinha.

items.p: Why do photos taken with a flash sometimes show red eyes?
opts: The flash bounces off the retina, which is full of blood vessels
items.why: The flash goes in through the wide-open pupil, bounces off the blood-rich retina and comes straight back to the camera. Picking 'the eyes make red light' mixes eyes up with light sources.

items.p: Why can't you see your own eyes without a mirror?
opts: Light from your eyes would have to bounce back into them, and nothing is there to bounce it
Your eyes are too close to see
items.why: To see something, light from it must reach your eyes. Light leaving the front of your eye goes away from you. A mirror bounces it back. Picking 'too close' is partly true, but even a camera needs to be pointed back at you. Picking 'invisible' is wrong, because other people can see your eyes.

items.p: Light from a faint star travels a very long way and enters your eye. Explain, using the word 'photon', what happens when it reaches your retina.
items.a: A photon from the star comes in through my pupil and lands on a rod cell in my retina. It hits a tiny molecule and makes it change shape. That starts a signal that goes along the optic nerve to my brain.
items.why: Every act of seeing starts with photons changing the shape of molecules in the retina.

items.p: A scallop has eyes with tiny mirrors instead of lenses. A plant has no eyes but bends to the light. What do all these ways of sensing light have in common?
opts: They all catch light that comes in
They all make their own light
items.why: Every eye and every light-sensing part catches light that arrives. None sends rays out. Some living things also make light, but that is a different unit.

items.p: Sort these statements about seeing.
items: We see when light enters our eyes.
The pupil shrinks in bright light.
Exactly how the brain turns signals into what we experience.
Whether a person can notice one single photon.
Rod cells work best in dim light.
Whether we see the world as it really is.
items.why: The path of light and the parts of the eye are well tested. How brains make experience, and the very edge of how sensitive we are, are still open.

items.p: Rupert Sheldrake says people can feel when they are being stared at. Why do most scientists disagree?
opts: Nothing comes out of the eyes to be felt, and careful tests found no effect
Because only cats can feel stares
items.why: Eyes catch light. They send nothing out. We tend to remember the times we turned and someone was looking, and forget the times nobody was. Other careful tests have found no effect.

items.p: Some people say 'the eye is just a camera'. Give one way the eye is like a camera, and one way it is different.
items.a: Like a camera: both have a hole that lets light in and a layer at the back that catches it. Different: the brain builds the picture from signals, fills in the blind spot and has to learn to see. A camera just records.
items.why: The camera idea helps with the front of the eye, but not with what the brain does.

items.p: After about 20 to 30 minutes in the dark, your eyes can become thousands of times more sensitive.
items.why: True. The rod cells slowly build up their light-catching chemical. This is why you see more stars after waiting.

items.p: In the blind spot activity, the dot vanished when the card was about 25 cm from your eye. If you moved the card to 50 cm, what would happen?
opts: The dot would come back, because its light no longer lands on the blind spot
The dot would stay hidden at every distance
items.why: The dot only vanishes when its light lands exactly on the blind spot. At other distances it lands on cells that can catch light, so you see it again.

items.p: Draw the room in the Ibn al-Haytham story: the dark room, the small hole, and the donkey outside in the sunlight. Draw arrows to show how the picture of the donkey got onto the wall.
items.a: An arrow from the Sun to the donkey, then arrows from the donkey through the hole to the wall.
items.why: Light from the Sun bounced off the donkey. Some of it came through the hole and landed on the wall.
items.art: An outline of a dark room with a small hole, and a donkey in a sunny street outside.

items.p: If light bounces off everything, why isn't every room full of images of everything, all mixed up?
items.a: Light from every point of every thing spreads out in all directions and mixes together in the room. That is why a white wall just looks bright, not like a picture. A small hole, or the pupil and lens of an eye, sorts the light so each point lands in one place. That makes a picture.
items.why: This is the puzzle Ibn al-Haytham worked on. Class 4 explains more about straight lines and holes.

items.p: Why do older people often need more light to read?
opts: Their lenses let less light through, and their pupils get smaller with age
Books were printed smaller long ago
items.why: As we grow old, the lens gets a little cloudy and yellow, and the pupil gets smaller. So less light reaches the retina. Picking 'weaker rays' is the old eye-rays idea.

items.p: Which idea is the deep truth of this unit?
opts: Seeing is receiving: the world's light comes into us
Seeing is reaching out to grab the world
Seeing happens only in the eyes
items.why: When we see, light that has bounced off the world comes into us. The eye catches it and the brain makes sense of it. Picking 'reaching out' is the old eye-rays idea. Picking 'only in the eyes' forgets the brain's big part.

items.p: Write two or three sentences for a younger child, explaining how they see their teddy bear.
items.a: The lamp shines light on your teddy. The light bounces off the teddy and goes into your eyes. Your eyes send a message to your brain, and your brain says 'teddy!'
items.why: A good answer has a source, a bounce, the eye and the brain, in the right order.

items.p: Label the parts of the eye on the drawing: cornea, iris, pupil, lens, retina, optic nerve.
items.a: Cornea at the very front, iris as the coloured ring, pupil as the hole in the middle, lens just behind it, retina lining the back, optic nerve leaving the back.
items.why: Light passes through these parts in order from front to back, and the optic nerve carries the signal on.

experiments.title: The Dark Box: can we see without light?
experiments.context: This is the dark box test. You hide three things in a closed shoebox and look through a small peephole. Then you let in a little light at a time.
experiments.question: Can we see anything when there is no light?
experiments.predict: Before you look, guess. What will you see through the peephole when the lid is shut tight? Which of the three things will you see first when a little light comes in?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, look through the same peephole every time, from the same place. Change only one thing: how far the lid is open. Look for the same count of 5 each time, because your eyes need a moment to settle.
results_table: Could I tell the ball's colour?

materials.item: a shoebox with a lid
scissors, used by a grown-up
a small piece of white paper, a steel spoon and a red ball or red bangle
black tape or a dark cloth to seal the gaps
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts the peephole. Do not put fingers near the scissors.

schedule.what: Make the box, guess what you will see, then open the lid a little at a time and record what appears.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw what you saw at each step: total dark, a crack of light, half open and fully open.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up cuts a round peephole, about as big as a one-rupee coin, in one short end of the shoebox. 2. Put the white paper, the steel spoon and the red ball inside, at the far end. Do this without your child watching. 3. Put the lid on and seal the edges with tape or a dark cloth.
flow.say: I've hidden three things inside this box. You're going to be a scientist and find out what you can see in there.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to cut a small hole in a shoebox. Then close your eyes. The grown-up hides three things inside. The lid goes on tight.
flow.context: This is the first step of the dark box test. You hide three things in a closed box, to find out whether we can see without light.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess before looking.
flow.say: When you look through the hole with the lid shut, what do you think you will see? If we let a little light in, what will you see first?
flow.kid: Guess first. What will you see with the lid shut? What will you see first when a little light gets in?

ask.q: What do you think you will see with the lid shut?
good: Maybe a little, if my eyes get used to it.

flow.do: 1. Your child puts one eye right against the peephole, and closes the other eye. 2. They count slowly to 5. 3. They say what they can see. 4. Write it in the table.
flow.say: Press your eye to the hole. Count slowly to five. What can you see?
flow.kid: Put one eye right on the hole. Close the other eye. Count to five. What can you see?
flow.parent: With the lid sealed, your child should see nothing at all. Some children say they see 'black'. That is a good observation. Black is what we call it when no light reaches the eye.

check.q: In the dark box with the lid shut, your eye is open but you see nothing. Why?
options: Your eye needs more time to send out its rays
No light is coming from the things into your eye
The things inside are too small
check.why: We see a thing only when light from it comes into our eyes. Inside a sealed box there is no light, so nothing bounces off the things and nothing comes to your eye. Picking 'send out its rays' is the very old idea that eyes reach out to see. If that were true, you would see in the box. Picking 'too small' misses the point, because you see them easily once the lid is open.

flow.do: 1. Lift one corner of the lid just a crack, about the width of a pencil. 2. Your child looks again and counts to 5. 3. Lift the lid halfway, and look again. 4. Take the lid off, and look again. 5. Each time, write down what they saw and whether they could tell the colour of the ball.
flow.say: Now I'll let in a tiny bit of light. What can you see now? Can you tell what colour the ball is?
flow.kid: A grown-up lifts the lid a crack. Look again. What appears first? Then a bit more light. Then all the way. Can you see the ball's colour yet?
flow.parent: Usually the white paper and the shiny spoon appear first, as pale grey shapes. The ball comes later, and its red colour last. White and shiny things bounce back the most light. The cells in the eye that see colour need more light than the ones that see shapes.

chart.title: Made-up example: how a filled-in table can look

flow.do: Compare what happened with the guesses from the start.
flow.say: Were your guesses right? Which thing showed up first, and why do you think it did?
flow.kid: Were you right? Which thing did you see first? Why do you think it came first?
flow.think: If you sat inside a cave with no light for an hour, would you start to see? Why or why not?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Let's finish like real scientists. Tell me what you think now, what you saw that shows it, and why you think it happened.
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: we need light to see. What I saw: with the lid shut I saw nothing, but when light came in I saw the paper first. Why: the things only show when light bounces off them into my eye.

experiments.title: Watch Your Pupils Change
experiments.context: In this test you watch the black circle in the middle of your eye, called the pupil, in a mirror. You measure how big it is in dim light and in bright light.
experiments.question: How does the size of my pupil change in dim light and in bright light?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will your pupil be bigger or smaller in dim light? Draw what you think it will look like in dim light and in bright light.
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, use the same mirror and the same eye each time. Change only one thing: how bright the room is. Wait the same time in each light, one full minute, before you measure. Measure three times in each light, because one look can be a fluke.

materials.item: a hand mirror
a printed pupil card: a row of black circles 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8 mm across, drawn on a strip of paper
a room you can make dim, and a table lamp
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Never shine the lamp or a torch straight into anyone's eyes. Never use the Sun. Point the lamp at the wall beside your face, not at your eyes.

schedule.what: Make the pupil card. Measure the pupil in dim light, room light and lamp light. Draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw a bar chart with one bar for each kind of light. Make each bar as tall as the middle pupil size.

flow.do: 1. On a strip of paper, draw a row of filled black circles. Make them 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8 mm across, using a ruler. 2. Write the size under each one. This is the pupil card.
flow.say: We're going to measure your pupil, the black circle in the middle of your eye. This card is our ruler. We'll hold it next to your eye and find the circle that matches.
flow.kid: Draw seven black circles in a row. Make them 2 to 8 mm wide. Write the size under each one. This is your pupil card.
flow.context: This is the first step of the pupil test. You watch the black circle in the middle of your eye in a mirror, and measure it in dim and bright light.

flow.do: 1. Make the room dim, with curtains closed and lights off, but bright enough to see your face in the mirror. 2. Wait one full minute. 3. Your child holds the mirror and the pupil card just under one eye. 4. They find the circle that matches the pupil. Write the size. Do this three times.
flow.say: Wait one minute for your eyes to settle. Now look in the mirror. Which circle on the card is the same size as your pupil?
flow.kid: Wait one minute in the dim room. Look at one eye in the mirror. Hold the card under it. Which circle matches the black middle? Write it down.
flow.parent: If it is hard for your child to see their own pupil, you can look at their eye and hold the card beside it. In dim light many children's pupils are 6 or 7 mm.

flow.do: 1. Turn on the normal room light and wait one minute. Measure three times. 2. Then switch on the lamp, pointing at the wall right beside your child's face, not into the eye. Wait one minute. Measure three times.
flow.say: Now the light is brighter. Watch your pupil closely as I switch the lamp on. What happens?
flow.kid: Now the light comes on. Watch your pupil as it does. What happens? Wait a minute. Measure it three times.

check.q: When the lamp came on, your pupil got smaller. Why does the eye do this?
options: To let in less light and protect the inside of the eye
Because the pupil is tired
To send out more light
check.why: The pupil is a hole that lets light in. In bright light the iris shrinks it, so that too much light does not dazzle the retina at the back. Picking 'tired' usually means thinking the eye is wearing out. It isn't. It opens again in the dark. Picking 'send out more light' is the old idea that eyes give out light. They don't.

flow.do: Help your child find the middle value for each light. Then draw a bar chart, with one bar for each kind of light.
flow.say: Let's turn the numbers into a picture. Each kind of light gets one bar. A taller bar means a bigger pupil.
flow.kid: Put your three numbers in order. The middle one is your middle value. Draw one bar for each light. A taller bar means a bigger pupil.

chart.title: Made-up example results: pupil size in different light
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences: what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: Tell me like a scientist. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? Why do you think your eye does this?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: my pupil gets smaller in bright light. What I saw: it was 7 mm in the dim room and 3 mm next to the lamp. Why: the pupil is a hole that lets in light, so it opens wide when there is little light and closes when there is a lot.
flow.think: Why do you think a cat's pupil can open even wider than yours?
