experiments.title: Break the Light's Journey
experiments.context: In this test you shine a torch on a toy in a dark room. Then you break the path of light in different places, to find out what seeing needs.
experiments.question: What do we need to see a thing that makes no light?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. If the torch is shining right on the toy, will you always be able to see it?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, keep the toy, the torch and your chair in the same places. Change only one thing each time: where the light's path is broken.
results_table: Is light landing on the toy?

materials.item: a torch
a small toy
a big piece of card or a hardback book
a room you can make very dark

experiments.safety: Never shine the torch into anyone's eyes.

schedule.what: Shine the torch on a toy. Break the light's path in three different places. Record what you can see.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw the toy, the torch and your eye. Draw the light's path with arrows, and mark where you broke it each time.

flow.do: 1. Put the toy on a table in a room you can make very dark. 2. Your child sits facing the toy, about two big steps away. 3. Turn off all the lights.
flow.say: The toy makes no light of its own. Let's find out exactly what we need to see it.
flow.kid: Put a toy on a table. Sit two big steps away, facing it. Turn off the lights. Can you see the toy?
flow.context: This is the first step of the light's journey test. You find out what you need to see a toy, by breaking the light's path in different places.

flow.do: 1. Shine the torch at the ceiling at the far side of the room. 2. Then shine it straight at the toy, from the side. 3. Each time, ask how well your child can see the toy.
flow.say: Now I'm shining the torch at the ceiling. Can you see the toy? Now I'm shining it right on the toy. How about now?
flow.kid: First the torch shines at the ceiling. Can you see the toy? Now it shines on the toy. Better?
flow.parent: With the torch on the ceiling, your child may just see the toy, because light bounces off the ceiling and lands on it. This is a good thing to notice. Light can bounce more than once.

flow.do: 1. Keep the torch shining on the toy. 2. Hold the card between the toy and your child's eyes. 3. Then hold the card between the torch and the toy instead.
flow.say: The torch is still shining on the toy. Now I put the card in front of your eyes. Can you see it? Now the card goes between the torch and the toy.
flow.kid: The torch still shines on the toy. A card goes in front of your eyes. Can you see the toy now? Now the card blocks the torch. What happens?

check.q: The torch is shining on the toy, but a card is in front of your eyes. Why can't you see the toy?
options: The toy has stopped being lit
Light bouncing off the toy can't reach your eyes
Your eyes have stopped working
check.why: The toy is still lit, and your eyes are fine. But the card stops the light that bounces off the toy from reaching your eyes. Seeing needs the whole journey: source, then thing, then eye. Picking 'the toy has stopped being lit' means looking only at the first half of the journey. Picking 'your eyes have stopped working' means thinking eyes see on their own.

flow.do: Turn off the torch, with nothing blocking anything.
flow.say: Last test. No card, but no torch. Can you see the toy?
flow.kid: Last test. The torch goes off. No card. Can you see the toy?

chart.title: Made-up example: a filled-in results table

flow.do: Ask your child to draw the torch, the toy and an eye with arrows, then say what they think, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Draw the light's path with arrows. Which way do the arrows go? Then tell me what you think, what you saw, and why.
flow.kid: Draw the torch, the toy and your eye. Draw arrows for the light. Then say: what I think, what I saw, why.
flow.parent: Look at the arrows. Many children draw an arrow from the eye to the toy. If your child does, ask: 'In the dark room, did your eye send something out? Then why couldn't you see?' A good answer: What I think: to see the toy, light must go from the torch to the toy and then into my eye. What I saw: when the card blocked either part, the toy vanished. Why: the toy makes no light, so it needs to bounce light from the torch into my eye.

activities.title: Catch the Invisible Beam
activities.context: In this activity you shine a torch across a dark room. The beam is almost invisible from the side, until you spray a fine mist into it.

materials.item: a bright torch
a plant spray bottle with water
a room you can make dark

activities.safety: Spray the mist away from faces and from anything electric. Wipe the floor afterwards so nobody slips.

schedule.what: Shine a torch across a dark room. Look at the beam from the side. Then spray mist into it.

activities.record: Draw the beam before the mist and after the mist. Draw arrows to show where the light goes to reach your eyes.

flow.do: 1. Make the room dark. 2. Put the torch on a table, shining across the room at a wall. 3. Your child stands to the side of the beam and looks at the air in between, not at the torch.
flow.say: The torch is shining across the room. Look at the air between the torch and the wall. Can you see the light travelling?
flow.kid: The torch shines across the dark room. Stand to the side. Look at the air in between. Can you see the beam?
flow.context: This is the first step of the invisible beam activity. You find out why a torch beam is hard to see from the side.

flow.do: Spray two or three puffs of mist into the air just above the beam, so the drops fall through it.
flow.say: Now watch the air when the mist falls through it.
flow.kid: A grown-up sprays mist above the beam. Watch the air. What do you see now?

ask.q: Why can you see the beam now?
good: The water drops bounce some light into my eyes.
The mist sends light sideways to me.

check.q: Before the mist, the torch beam was hard to see from the side. Why?
options: The light was going straight to the wall, not into your eyes
Light is too fast to see
The torch was too weak
check.why: We see light only when it comes into our eyes. In clean air the beam travels straight to the wall, and almost none of it turns sideways towards you. Mist drops bounce some light in all directions, and some of it reaches your eyes. Picking 'too fast' is a common idea, but speed is not the problem. Picking 'too weak' doesn't fit, because the spot on the wall is bright.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw the beam before and after the mist, with arrows showing where the light goes.
flow.say: Draw what you saw. Then draw arrows. Which way did the light go to reach your eyes?
flow.kid: Draw the beam with no mist, and with mist. Add arrows. How did the light get to your eyes?
flow.think: Sunbeams in a dusty room, or through trees on a misty morning, work the same way. Where else have you seen a beam of light?
flow.parent: A good answer: each drop of mist bounces a little light sideways, into my eyes. Without the drops, the light went straight past me to the wall.

activities.title: Find Your Blind Spot
activities.context: Everyone has a blind spot in each eye, where no light can be caught. In this activity you find yours with a cross and a dot on a card.

materials.item: a white card or paper, about the size of a postcard
a black pen
a 30 cm ruler

activities.safety: No safety worries. Take a break if your eye feels tired.

schedule.what: Make the card. Find the blind spot in each eye. Measure how far away the card is when the dot vanishes.

activities.record: Write how far the card was from your eye when the dot vanished, for your right eye and your left eye. Ask a family member to try too.

flow.do: On the card, draw a small cross on the left and a filled dot about as big as a pea on the right. Put them about 8 cm apart, on the same line.
flow.say: We're going to find a place in your eye that cannot see at all. Everyone has one. This card will show us.
flow.kid: Draw a small cross on the left of the card. Draw a black dot on the right, 8 cm away. Make them the same height.
flow.context: This is the first step of the blind spot activity. You draw a cross and a dot on a card to find the place in your eye that cannot catch light.

flow.do: 1. Your child covers their left eye with their hand. 2. They hold the card at arm's length and stare at the cross with the right eye. 3. They slowly bring the card closer, still staring at the cross. 4. When the dot disappears, stop. Measure from the eye to the card with the ruler.
flow.say: Keep looking only at the cross. Don't look at the dot. Bring the card slowly closer. Tell me the moment the dot vanishes.
flow.kid: Cover your left eye. Stare at the cross with your right eye. Bring the card slowly closer. Does the dot vanish? Stop there!
flow.parent: The dot usually vanishes when the card is about 20 to 30 cm from the eye. If it doesn't, check your child is staring at the cross, not the dot. For the left eye, cover the right eye and stare at the dot instead. The cross will vanish.

flow.do: Talk about why the dot vanished, and what your child saw in its place.
flow.say: When the dot vanished, what did you see where it had been? A black hole, or plain white card?
flow.kid: When the dot vanished, what was there instead? A hole? Or plain white card?

check.q: When the dot vanished, you saw plain white card, not a hole. Why?
options: Your brain filled in the gap with what is around it
The dot really disappeared from the card
Your eye sent out a ray that rubbed it out
check.why: The dot's light landed on your blind spot, where the optic nerve leaves the eye and there are no light-catching cells. Your brain does not like gaps. It fills the hole with what is around it, plain white card. Picking 'the dot really disappeared' is easy to check: open both eyes and it is back. Picking 'the eye sent out a ray' is the old eye-rays idea. Eyes do not send anything out.

flow.think: You walk around all day with two holes in your sight, and you never notice. What else might your brain be filling in?

activities.title: Night Eyes: 20 minutes in the dark
activities.context: In this activity you sit outside on a dark night and count stars at the start, after 10 minutes and after 20 minutes. You find out how your eyes get used to the dark.

materials.item: a cardboard tube from a roll of kitchen paper or foil
a torch with red cellophane taped over the front
a mat to sit on, and a notebook
a clock or phone with the screen turned down

activities.safety: A grown-up must be with the child on a terrace, roof or in a garden at night. Stay well away from the edge of any roof.

schedule.what: On a clear evening, go to the darkest place nearby. Count stars through a tube at 0, 10 and 20 minutes.

activities.record: Write the number of stars you counted through the tube at the start, after 10 minutes and after 20 minutes. Draw a bar chart.

flow.do: 1. On a clear night, go with your child to the darkest place you can reach, like a terrace or a garden. 2. Turn off any lights you can. 3. Pick one patch of sky. Look at it through the cardboard tube, and count the stars you see.
flow.say: Look through the tube at this patch of sky. Count every star you can see. We'll count again in a while and see if anything changes.
flow.kid: With a grown-up, go somewhere dark at night. Look at the sky through the tube. Count the stars you see. Write the number.
flow.context: This is the first step of the night eyes activity. You count stars through a tube to find out how your eyes change in the dark.

flow.do: 1. Sit quietly for 10 minutes. Do not look at a phone or a white light. If you need to see your notebook, use the red torch. 2. Count the stars in the same patch again. 3. Wait 10 more minutes and count once more.
flow.say: No bright lights now, not even a phone. A bright light would spoil your night eyes. We'll use only the red torch. Let's count again.
flow.kid: Sit still for 10 minutes. No phone, no bright light. Use only the red torch. Then count the stars again. Wait 10 more minutes. Count again.
flow.parent: Most people count more stars at 10 minutes and even more at 20. The pupils open wide in a few seconds, but the bigger change is the rod cells building up their light-catching chemical. Red light disturbs the rods less than white light does. While you wait, tell your child about the story of Ibn al-Haytham, or play a quiet guessing game about night sounds.

flow.do: Back inside, help your child draw a bar chart of the three counts, and say what they think, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Let's make a bar for each count. What happened to the number of stars? The sky didn't change, so what did?
flow.kid: Draw a bar for each count. Did the number go up? The sky stayed the same. So what changed?

check.q: You counted more stars after 20 minutes in the dark. What changed?
options: More stars came out
Your eyes became more sensitive to dim light
Your eyes started making their own light
check.why: The stars were there all along. In the dark, your pupils opened wide and your rod cells slowly got much better at catching faint light. So dim stars that were too faint at first became visible. Picking 'more stars came out' is a natural guess, but the sky barely changes in 20 minutes. Picking 'eyes making their own light' mixes up eyes with light sources. Eyes only catch light.

activities.title: Ibn al-Haytham's Lamps
activities.context: About a thousand years ago, Ibn al-Haytham put lamps outside a small hole into a dark room. In this activity you do the same with torches and a shoebox.

materials.item: a shoebox
aluminium foil and tape
tracing paper or baking paper
a pin or a sharp pencil, used by a grown-up
3 torches, or 3 phone torches
a dark cloth or towel

activities.safety: A grown-up makes the holes. Never shine the torches into anyone's eyes.

schedule.what: Make the box. Shine three torches at the pinhole. Cover one torch at a time and watch its spot.

activities.record: Draw the three spots on the screen. Then draw what happened when you covered each torch.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up cuts a square hole, about 3 cm wide, in one short end of the shoebox, and tapes foil over it. 2. They make one small hole in the foil with a pin or pencil tip. 3. Cut away the other short end and tape tracing paper over it. This is the screen.
flow.say: We're going to make a little dark room, like Ibn al-Haytham's. Light can only get in through one tiny hole.
flow.kid: A grown-up makes a small hole in foil on the box. Tape tracing paper over the other end. That is your screen.
flow.context: This is the first step of Ibn al-Haytham's lamps. You make a dark box with one small hole, to find out where light goes.

flow.do: 1. Make the room dark. 2. Stand three torches in a row on a table, about one hand apart, all pointing at the pinhole. 3. Put the box about half a metre away. 4. Your child looks at the tracing-paper screen, with the dark cloth over their head and the end of the box.
flow.say: Look at the screen. How many spots of light can you see?
flow.kid: Turn on three torches in a row. Point them at the hole. Put the cloth over your head. Look at the screen. How many spots?
flow.parent: You should see three small spots of light on the screen, one for each torch. Notice that the order is swapped. The left torch makes the right spot. That is because light travels in straight lines through the hole, which you learn about in Class 4. Today we only need: each torch makes its own spot.

flow.do: Cover one torch with your hand. Your child watches the screen and says which spot vanished. Then try the other torches.
flow.say: I'm covering one torch now. What happened on the screen?
flow.kid: A grown-up covers one torch. Watch the screen. What happened? Try each torch.

check.q: When one torch was covered, only one spot went out. What does that show?
options: Each torch's light travels from the torch into the box
The box makes the light itself
Your eye sends out three rays
check.why: Each spot is made by light that travelled from one torch, through the hole, to the screen. Block that torch and its light never arrives. Ibn al-Haytham used this to show light goes from things to where it lands, not the other way. Picking 'the box makes the light' doesn't fit, because the spots go out when the torches do. Picking 'your eye sends out rays' doesn't fit either. Your eye did not change, but a spot vanished.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they think, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Like Ibn al-Haytham, tell me: what do you think now about where light goes? What did you see? Why?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer: What I think: light goes from each torch into the box. What I saw: when one torch was covered, only its spot vanished. Why: each torch sends its own light, and blocking it stops that light arriving. Your eye works the same way: it is a dark room with a small hole, the pupil.
flow.think: Your eye is a small dark room with a hole at the front. What is the 'screen' inside your eye called?

activities.title: Eyeshine and Red Eyes
activities.context: In this activity you look for glowing eyes at night, and red eyes in flash photos. You find out that the glow is light bouncing back, not light made by the eye.

materials.item: a torch
a phone camera with a flash

activities.safety: A grown-up comes on the evening walk. Stay far from street dogs and never disturb an animal. Never shine a torch into a person's eyes.

schedule.what: On an evening walk, look for eyeshine with a torch held next to your eyes. At home, take a flash photo in dim light and look for red eyes.

activities.record: Draw an animal with eyeshine. Draw an arrow from the torch to the eye, and an arrow bouncing back to you.

flow.do: 1. On an evening walk, hold the torch right beside your own eyes, pointing ahead. 2. Look for a pair of glowing dots in the dark, from a cat, a dog or a cow. 3. Stay far away from the animal and keep walking calmly.
flow.say: Hold the torch right next to your eyes. If an animal's eyes are out there, they will flash back at us. Do the eyes glow when we turn the torch off?
flow.kid: Go on an evening walk with a grown-up. Hold the torch next to your eyes. Look for glowing eyes. Turn the torch off. Do they still glow?
flow.context: This is the first step of the eyeshine activity. You look for animal eyes that seem to glow at night, to find out where the glow comes from.

flow.do: 1. At home, dim the room. 2. Take a flash photo of a family member looking straight at the phone. 3. Look at their eyes in the photo.
flow.say: Look at the eyes in the photo. Are they red? The flash went in through the pupil and bounced back off the back of the eye.
flow.kid: Take a flash photo of someone in a dim room. Look at their eyes. Are they red?
flow.parent: Many phones now try to remove red eye, so you may need a few tries. Red eye happens because the retina at the back of the eye is full of tiny blood vessels. The flash bounces off it, straight back to the camera.

flow.do: Ask what the glowing eyes and the red eyes have in common.
flow.say: When you turned off the torch, did the eyes still glow? So were they making light, or bouncing it?
flow.kid: Did the eyes glow with the torch off? So do eyes make light, or bounce it?

check.q: A cat's eyes glow in your torch beam. Where does the glow come from?
options: The cat's eyes make their own light
Your torch's light bounces off a shiny layer at the back of the cat's eye
The cat is sending out rays to see you
check.why: Cats have a shiny layer behind the retina. It bounces light back through the retina for a second chance to be caught, which helps cats see in dim light. Some of that light comes back out to you. Turn off the torch, and the glow stops. Picking 'makes its own light' is very common, but cats' eyes are not light sources. Picking 'sending out rays' is the old eye-rays idea.

activities.title: Draw How You See
activities.context: In this activity you draw a picture of how you see a thing, with arrows. You draw it at the start of the unit and again at the end, and compare.

materials.item: paper and coloured pencils

schedule.what: Draw how you see a ball, before learning about it. Draw it again at the end of the unit, and compare.

activities.record: Keep both drawings side by side. Write one sentence on what changed.

flow.do: Before teaching anything, ask your child to draw themselves looking at a ball, with a lamp in the room. Ask them to add arrows to show how they see the ball.
flow.say: Draw yourself looking at a ball. There's a lamp in the room too. Now add arrows to show how you see the ball. There's no right or wrong yet.
flow.kid: Draw yourself looking at a ball. Draw a lamp too. Add arrows to show how you see the ball.
flow.parent: Do not correct the drawing. Many children draw an arrow from their eye to the ball, or no arrows at all. Both are the ideas people had for thousands of years. Keep the drawing.
flow.context: This is the first step of the drawing activity. You draw how you think you see a ball, before you learn about it.

flow.do: At the end of the unit, ask your child to draw the same picture again, without looking at the first one.
flow.say: Draw the same picture again: you, a ball and a lamp. Add arrows to show how you see the ball.
flow.kid: Draw it again: you, a ball and a lamp. Add arrows. How do you see the ball?

check.q: Which drawing shows how you see a ball in a lit room?
options: An arrow from the lamp to the ball, and from the ball to the eye
An arrow from the eye to the ball
An arrow from the lamp to the eye only
check.why: Light goes from the lamp to the ball. It bounces off the ball and travels into your eye. Picking 'eye to ball' is the old eye-rays idea. Picking 'lamp to eye only' explains how you see the lamp, but not the ball.

flow.do: Put both drawings side by side and talk about what changed.
flow.say: Look at both drawings. What's different? What made you change your mind?
flow.kid: Put your two drawings side by side. What changed? What made you change your mind?
flow.think: Scientists change their drawings when they find new evidence. What was your evidence?

projects.title: Eye in a Box
projects.context: In this 2-day project you build a model eye from a shoebox. It has a pupil you can make bigger or smaller, and a paper retina at the back where the light lands.

materials.item: a shoebox
aluminium foil, tape and glue
tracing paper or baking paper
a strip of stiff card, about 4 cm by 20 cm, for the iris slider
a pencil, a pin and scissors, used by a grown-up
a piece of wool or string, for the optic nerve
a table lamp
colours, to paint the iris

projects.safety: A grown-up does all the cutting. Never look at the Sun through the box or any hole.

schedule.what: Build the box eye: the cornea window, the iris slider with three pupil sizes, and the retina screen. Paint the iris.
Test the eye in a dark room with a lamp. Try each pupil size. Label the parts and show the family how it works.

projects.record: Draw what you saw on the retina screen with the small, middle and big pupil. Label the parts of your box eye.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up cuts a 3 cm square window in one short end of the box and tapes clear plastic or nothing over it. This is the cornea. 2. Cut away the other short end and tape tracing paper over it. This is the retina screen. 3. Cut two slits above and below the front window, so the card strip can slide across it.
flow.say: We're building an eye. The front window is the cornea. The paper at the back is the retina, where the light lands.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts a window in the front of the box. Tape tracing paper over the back. That is the retina. Cut slits so a card strip can slide across the front.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Eye in a Box project. You build a model eye from a shoebox, with a pupil and a retina.

flow.do: 1. On the card strip, a grown-up makes three round holes: one as small as a pin, one as big as a pea, one as big as a coin. 2. Your child paints a coloured ring around each hole. This is the iris. 3. Slide the strip into the slits. 4. Tape the string to the back of the box and lead it to a drawing of a brain. This is the optic nerve.
flow.say: These three holes are pupils of different sizes. The coloured ring around each is the iris. The string is the optic nerve, which carries signals to the brain.
flow.kid: A grown-up makes three holes in the card: tiny, middle, big. Paint a coloured ring around each one. That is the iris. Slide it in. Tape on a string to a brain drawing.

flow.wait: Leave the paint to dry until tomorrow.
flow.do: 1. On day 2, make the room dark and switch on a lamp at one end. 2. Your child holds the box with the front pointing at the lamp, and looks at the retina screen. 3. Slide the strip to try each pupil size. Draw what you see each time.
flow.say: Try the tiny pupil first. What's on the retina? Now the big pupil. What's different?
flow.kid: Point the front of the box at the lamp. Look at the screen at the back. Try the tiny hole, then the middle, then the big one. What changes?
flow.parent: With the tiny hole, your child may see a dim but sharp glowing picture of the lamp. With the big hole, it is brighter but blurry. A real eye has a lens behind the pupil, which keeps the picture sharp even when the pupil is big. Another unit explains how lenses work.

check.q: In your box eye, which pupil lets the most light land on the retina?
options: The big hole
The tiny hole
They all let in the same amount
check.why: A bigger hole lets more light through, so the retina screen glows brighter. That is why your real pupil opens wide in the dark. Picking 'the tiny hole' may come from noticing its picture looks sharper. Sharp is not the same as bright. Picking 'the same amount' misses how much brighter the big hole makes the screen.

flow.do: Help your child label the box eye: cornea, iris, pupil, retina and optic nerve. Then they show it to the family and explain how we see.
flow.say: Now you're the teacher. Show the family your eye and tell them how light gets in and where it lands.
flow.kid: Label the parts. Then show your family. Tell them how light gets into the eye, and where it lands.
flow.think: Your box eye catches light, but it sends no signals on. What does a real eye have that the box doesn't?

challenges.title: Light the Reading Corner Without a Bulb
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You must make a dim corner of your home bright enough to read in, using only daylight bounced from a window.
challenges.problem: One corner of your home is too dark to read in during the day. Make it bright enough to read a reading card, using only daylight that comes in through a window. You cannot switch on any lamp.
constraints: Use only things you find at home.
Test with the same reading card each time, from the same chair.
materials: a reading card: a sheet with 6 lines of writing, each line smaller than the one above
white chart paper or a white bedsheet
cardboard, tape and books to prop things up
general: Hang a white sheet or white chart paper where the window light hits it. White things bounce a lot of light in every direction, some into the dark corner.
Paint or cover the walls near the corner in white or a pale colour. Dark walls swallow light. Pale walls bounce it on.
Open the curtains fully, and move anything that blocks the window.
creative: Prop a sheet of foil or a steel plate to bounce a patch of sunlight onto the white ceiling above the corner. The ceiling then spreads it around.
In some villages and towns, people have made solar bottle lights: a clear bottle of water fixed through a tin roof. It carries daylight down into a dark room.
Use several white boards in a chain, each one bouncing light a bit further round the corner.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own way to bring light into the corner. Draw it, build it and test it with the reading card. How many lines can you read now?

flow.do: 1. Make a reading card with 6 lines of writing, each line smaller than the one above. 2. Sit in the dark corner and count how many lines your child can read.
flow.say: First, let's measure. How many lines can you read in this corner right now?
flow.kid: Make a card with 6 lines of writing, big to small. Sit in the dark corner. How many lines can you read?
flow.context: This is the first step of the reading corner challenge. You measure how dark the corner is before you try to bring in daylight.

flow.do: 1. Try one idea at a time, like a white sheet near the window or foil bouncing light onto the ceiling. 2. After each idea, count the lines your child can read. 3. Write it down.
flow.say: Try one idea at a time, so we know which one helps. After each one, read the card again.
flow.kid: Try one idea. Read the card again. How many lines now? Write it down. Then try the next idea.
flow.parent: Changing one thing at a time makes it a fair test. White and pale things usually help a lot, because they bounce light in every direction. Shiny foil helps only if it is aimed carefully. Never aim bounced sunlight into anyone's eyes.

flow.do: Ask your child to explain why the best idea worked, using the words 'bounce' and 'eye'.
flow.say: Which idea worked best? Tell me the path the light took, from the window all the way into your eyes.
flow.kid: Which idea worked best? Tell the path of the light. From the window, to what, to the card, to your eyes.

check.q: A white sheet near the window made the corner brighter. Why?
options: The white sheet makes its own light
Daylight bounces off the white sheet in every direction, some of it into the corner
The white sheet keeps the dark away
check.why: White things bounce back most of the light that lands on them, spraying it in every direction. Some of that light lands on the reading card and then bounces into your eyes. Picking 'makes its own light' mixes up a lit thing with a light source. Picking 'keeps the dark away' treats darkness as a thing. Darkness is only missing light.

challenges.title: A Night Path for Nani
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You must help a grandparent find the way from bed to the bathroom at night, without a bright light that wakes everyone up.
challenges.problem: Nani gets up at night to go to the bathroom. When the light is switched on, everyone wakes up, and her eyes are dazzled. With the light off, she cannot see the step or the door. Design a way for her to see the path safely.
constraints: It must not wake people sleeping in the room.
It must not dazzle Nani's eyes when she has been asleep.
Use things that are safe, cheap and easy to find.
materials: card, scissors and a torch for testing
general: Put a small dim night-light low down near the floor. A dim light keeps her night eyes working, and does not dazzle.
Stick white tape along the edge of the step and around the door frame. Pale things bounce the most of what little light there is, so they show up first in the dark.
Clear the path of things she could trip on.
creative: Use a dim red or orange night-light. Our night eyes are less disturbed by red light, which is why astronomers use red torches.
A light that switches on by itself when someone walks past, then turns off again.
Glow-in-the-dark stickers along the wall, at hand height, like a trail of stars.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own night path. Draw a map of the room with your ideas on it. Test it at night with a grown-up. Can someone walk the path with only your design to see by?

flow.do: 1. At night, with the lights off, stand at Nani's bed with your child. 2. Wait a minute. 3. Ask what they can see along the path, and what they can't.
flow.say: Let's see the room the way Nani sees it at night. What can you see? What's invisible?
flow.kid: At night, stand by the bed with a grown-up. Turn the lights off. Wait a minute. What can you see? What can't you see?
flow.context: This is the first step of the night path challenge. You find out what a grandparent can and cannot see when walking at night.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws a map of the room and marks their ideas. 2. Try one idea at a time, like white tape on the step. 3. Check it again in the dark.
flow.say: Draw the room and mark your ideas. Then let's try them one at a time and see which ones work.
flow.kid: Draw a map of the room. Mark your ideas. Try one at a time in the dark. Which one helps most?
flow.parent: Remind your child of the dark box test. The white paper showed up first in dim light. The same is true of white tape on a step. Older people often need more light to see than children do, because their lenses let less light through.

flow.do: Ask your child to explain why their best idea works, using what they know about light and eyes.
flow.say: Why does your idea work? Tell me what the light does, and what Nani's eyes do.
flow.kid: Why does your idea work? Say what the light does. Say what Nani's eyes do.

check.q: Why does white tape on the edge of a step help someone see it at night?
options: White tape bounces back more of the little light there is
White tape makes its own light
White tape helps eyes send out rays
check.why: In dim light, pale things bounce back the most light, so they reach our eyes first. That is why the white paper showed up first in the dark box. Picking 'makes its own light' mixes up a lit thing with a light source, like a night-light. Picking 'helps eyes send out rays' is the old eye-rays idea.

quiz.p: When do we see a thing that makes no light, like a book?
opts: When light bounces off it into our eyes
When our eyes send out rays to it
quiz.why: Lit things are seen when light from a source bounces off them into our eyes. Picking 'eyes send out rays' is the old eye-rays idea. Picking 'whenever our eyes are open' forgets that we see nothing in total darkness.

quiz.p: Which of these is NOT a light source?
quiz.why: The Moon makes no light of its own. It is a rock lit by the Sun. The others all make their own light.

quiz.p: You are in a room with no light at all, with your eyes wide open. What do you see?
quiz.why: With no light, there is nothing for the eye to catch. Grey shapes appear only when there is a little light. Waiting helps in dim light, not in total darkness.

quiz.p: Which drawing shows how you see a tree in sunshine?
quiz.why: Sunlight lands on the tree, bounces off it, and goes into the eye. An arrow from the eye to the tree is the old eye-rays idea.

quiz.p: Which part of the eye is a hole that lets light in?
quiz.why: The pupil is the hole in the middle of the iris. The retina catches light at the back, and the optic nerve carries signals to the brain.

quiz.p: What happens to your pupil when you walk into bright sunshine?
quiz.why: In bright light the iris shrinks the pupil to protect the eye. In dim light it opens wide. The colour of the iris does not change.

quiz.p: In the pupil test, why did we measure three times in each light?
opts: Because one look can be a fluke
Because the pupil needs three tries to work
quiz.why: Doing a test more than once makes the result more trustworthy. One look might be a mistake. The pupil works every time, but our measuring might not.

quiz.p: Why can't you see a toy when a card is in front of your eyes, even though a torch shines on it?
opts: The card stops the toy's bounced light reaching your eyes
quiz.why: The toy is still lit and your eyes are fine. But the light from the toy cannot reach your eyes. Seeing needs the whole journey.

quiz.p: Long ago people thought eyes send out rays. Which clue shows they were wrong?
opts: We can't see in a totally dark room, even with our eyes open
quiz.why: If eyes sent out rays, we would see in the dark. Blinking and glasses don't tell us which way light goes.

quiz.p: Who showed, about a thousand years ago in Cairo, that light comes into the eye?
quiz.why: Ibn al-Haytham wrote the Book of Optics in Cairo. Newton lived about 650 years later. Aristotle had a similar direction but not the tests and details.

quiz.p: Why did the dot vanish in the blind spot activity, without leaving a hole?
opts: Its light landed where there are no light-catching cells, and the brain filled in the gap
The eye sent a ray that hid it
quiz.why: The blind spot is where the optic nerve leaves the eye. The brain fills the gap with what is around it.
Light comes in tiny packets called photons. A rod cell in the retina can respond to a single one.

quiz.p: Which of these do scientists still NOT know?
opts: Exactly how the brain turns signals from the eyes into what we experience
quiz.why: Light entering the eye and the pupil changing size are well tested. How the brain turns signals into experience is one of the biggest open questions.

quiz.p: A cat's eyes glow in a car's headlights. Why?
opts: The headlights' light bounces off a shiny layer inside the cat's eyes
Cats can see in total darkness
quiz.why: Eyeshine is bounced light. Cats see well in dim light, but not in total darkness, and their eyes make no light.

applications: Eye doctors look through the pupil at the retina with a bright light, to check that eyes are healthy.

Cataract surgery replaces a cloudy lens with a clear one. Aravind Eye Hospital in Madurai, started in 1976 by Dr G. Venkataswamy with his sister Dr G. Natchiar and others, has done millions of these operations, many of them free.
An old Indian medical book, the Sushruta Samhita, describes an early operation to push a cloudy lens out of the way.
Cameras, including phone cameras, work by letting light in through a hole and catching it at the back, like an eye.
Night drivers rely on headlights bouncing light off the road, animals and signs into their eyes.
Pale or white paint on walls and ceilings makes rooms brighter, because it bounces more light around.
Astronomers use dim red torches to protect their night eyes.
Safety stripes on steps, kerbs and speed breakers are painted white or yellow, so they bounce enough light to be seen at dusk.
Doctors check the pupils with a small torch after a head injury, because pupils should shrink in light.
Sunglasses and caps protect the eyes by cutting down the light that comes in.
Eye tests at school use a chart of letters getting smaller, to find out how sharply each child sees.
Project Prakash in India helps children born with treatable blindness to see, and studies how the brain learns to see.

open_questions.q: How does the brain turn signals from the eyes into the experience of seeing?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know which parts of the brain are busy when we see. But nobody knows how those signals become the feeling of seeing a red mango. Some call this 'the hard problem'.

open_questions.q: Can a person notice just one single photon?
open_questions.why_open: One study in 2016 said yes, sometimes. The result was small, and other teams need to repeat it.

open_questions.q: Do other animals experience seeing the way we do?
open_questions.why_open: We can measure what a bee's or an octopus's eyes respond to. We cannot get inside their experience.

open_questions.q: Exactly how many times did eyes appear separately in the history of life?
open_questions.why_open: Many scientists think eyes appeared dozens of times. But some of the genes for building eyes are shared by very different animals, so the history is still argued about.

open_questions.q: Why do most people sometimes see faces in clouds and in the fronts of cars?
open_questions.why_open: The brain is quick to find faces. Scientists are still working out exactly how and why it does this so readily.

open_questions.q: How do children who gain sight late learn to see so quickly?
open_questions.why_open: Project Prakash found many learn faster than expected. Exactly how the brain does this is still being studied.

maths.problem: In the pupil test, a child's pupil was 7 mm in the dim room and 3 mm next to the lamp. How many millimetres smaller did it get?
maths.explain: The pupil started at 7 mm in dim light. Next to the lamp it was 3 mm. 7 take away 3 is 4. So it shrank by 4 mm. You can check: 3 + 4 = 7.
maths.context: This is about the pupil test. You measured the black circle in the middle of your eye, called the pupil, in dim light and in bright light, using a card of black circles.

chart.title: Pupil size in two kinds of light

maths.why_maths: Saying 'it got smaller' is a start. Taking away tells us exactly how much smaller, so we can compare with other people's eyes.

maths.problem: In the pupil test, a child measured three times in the dim room: 6 mm, 7 mm and 7 mm. What is the middle value?
maths.explain: Put the three numbers in order: 6, 7, 7. The middle one is the second number, which is 7. So the middle value is 7 mm.
maths.context: In the pupil test, you measure your pupil three times in each light, because one look can be a fluke. Then you choose one number to stand for all three.
maths.why_maths: Three measurements are more trustworthy than one. Putting them in order and taking the middle one gives a fair single answer.

maths.problem: In the night eyes activity, a child counted 3 stars at the start, 7 after 10 minutes and 11 after 20 minutes. How many more stars could they see after 20 minutes than at the start?
maths.explain: At the start they saw 3 stars. After 20 minutes they saw 11. 11 take away 3 is 8. So they could see 8 more stars. The sky did not change. Their eyes did.
maths.context: This is about the night eyes activity. You sat in the dark and counted stars through a cardboard tube at the start, after 10 minutes and after 20 minutes.
maths.why_maths: The bar chart shows the counts going up. Subtracting tells us exactly how much better the child's night eyes got.

maths.problem: In the blind spot activity, the dot vanished when the card was 25 cm from the eye. Read the ruler in the picture. Is the card nearer or further than a 30 cm ruler's length?
maths.explain: The card was 25 cm away. A whole ruler is 30 cm. 25 is less than 30, so the card was nearer. 30 take away 25 is 5. So it was 5 cm nearer than a ruler's length.
maths.context: This is about the blind spot activity. You drew a cross and a dot on a card, covered one eye, and moved the card closer until the dot vanished. Then you measured from your eye to the card.

chart.title: A 30 cm ruler from the eye to the card
chart.label: Each small mark is 1 cm.

maths.why_maths: Measuring in centimetres lets you compare your blind spot distance with your family's, and check whether everyone's is about the same.

maths.problem: In the dark box test, 0 of the 3 things were seen with the lid shut, 2 with a crack open and 3 with the lid off. What fraction of the things could be seen with the lid open a crack?
maths.explain: There were 3 things in the box. With the lid open a crack, 2 of them could be seen. So 2 out of 3 were seen. We write this as two thirds.
maths.context: This is about the dark box test. You hid three things in a shoebox and looked through a peephole, letting in a little light at a time.

chart.title: Things seen in the dark box (out of 3)

maths.why_maths: A fraction shows how much of the whole group we could see. It turns 'some of them' into an exact answer.

roots.context: We have been learning how we see: light bounces off things and comes into our eyes. Now we ask what seeing tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Seeing is receiving. The world comes into you.
deep_truth.habit: We think of looking as something we do to the world, reaching out from inside us. But nothing goes out. Light that touched the mango a moment ago is now inside your eye. The line between 'me in here' and 'the world out there' is crossed every time you see.
deep_truth.evidence: In the dark box, open eyes saw nothing until light came in. When a torch was covered, only its own spot went out.

three.who_am_i: You are a light catcher. Part of the world arrives in you every time you open your eyes.
three.what_is_life: Almost every living thing, from a plant on a windowsill to an owl, lives by catching light.
three.what_is_this_world: Everything is always sending out light to everything else, whether anyone is looking or not.

roots.thread: One Sun sends out light. That one light lands on mangoes, faces, rivers and cows, and bounces off each in its own way. So the many things we see are all lit by the same light. When it reaches us, our eyes and brains turn it back into a picture of the many. DeepKids believes this is the One showing up as many, and the many coming home again inside each of us.

teachings.teaching: King Janaka asks the sage Yajnavalkya: 'What light does a person live by?' The Sun, says Yajnavalkya. When the Sun has set? The Moon. When the Moon has set? Fire. When the fire has gone out? Speech, a voice to follow. And when all of these are gone? Then the self is the person's own light.
teachings.link: We have learned that eyes see only by outside light, from the Sun, the Moon or a fire. The sage asks about a different kind of light: the awareness that knows the seeing.

teachings.teaching: It is the ear of the ear, the mind of the mind, and the eye of the eye.
teachings.link: The eye catches light, and the brain makes sense of it. But who, or what, is aware of the seeing? The Upanishad points to something behind the eye.

teachings.teaching: The Buddha's teaching, as told by his student Mahakaccana: depending on the eye and on what is seen, seeing arises. The meeting of the three is called contact.
teachings.link: Seeing is not owned by the eye alone, or by the thing alone. It arises when they meet. Science adds one more thing they need: light. Take the light away, as in the dark box, and seeing does not arise.

science.text: We see only when light from things enters our eyes and lands on the retina, which sends signals to the brain.
How the brain turns those signals into the experience of seeing is not known. Scientists call this an open problem.

other_view.who: Many neuroscientists, and the philosopher Daniel Dennett
other_view.view: Seeing is just the eye and brain processing light. There is no little watcher inside the head, and no need for an 'eye of the eye'. When we understand the brain well enough, there will be nothing left to explain. That is an honest view, and many careful people hold it.

practice.title: Let the light come in
practice.say: Let's sit by the window. Close your eyes and take three slow breaths. Now open them very slowly. Don't look at anything in particular. Just let the light come to you. Notice that you don't have to do anything to see. The room arrives by itself. Now close your eyes again. Where did the room go? Open them once more, and welcome it back.
practice.kid: Sit by a window. Close your eyes. Breathe slowly three times. Open them very slowly. Don't try to look. Let the light come in to you. Close them again. Open once more.
